screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Sports Medicine & Injury queue positions 4-93. Drafted by Claude Haiku 5.5 and claim-audited against source text by Claude Opus 5.5 (docs/haiku-calibration/).

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Photobiomodulation therapy as a tool to prevent hamstring strain injuries by reducing soccer-induced fatigue on hamstring muscles.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 12 male amateur soccer players (mean age 25 years). Each player received photobiomodulation (300 J per thigh) or placebo before a 45-minute simulated match, with sessions at least 7 days apart. Hamstring eccentric peak torque fell 4.85% after PBMT and 8.72% after placebo, and the H:Q ratio fell 3.60% after PBMT (P = .056) and 7.75% after placebo (P = .008).
records.limitations: Twelve amateur players, one PBMT dose and one 45-minute simulated protocol, with acute strength and jump outcomes only. No injury outcomes were measured, so the injury-prevention claim is an extrapolation.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the smaller acute strength loss after PBMT as evidence that PBMT prevents hamstring injuries, which the study did not measure.

changes: limitations: conflict of interest misdescribed as two authors with 'one is an employee and shareholder' -> Leal-Junior 'receives research support' and Johnson 'is an employee and shareholder', with the authors' statement that they had no role in data collection or analysis
limitations: added dominant-limb-only isokinetic testing ('knee flexion-extension movements with the dominant limb') and the non-significant within-condition CMJ change

records.sourceFile: Physician perceptions of cannabidiol and cannabis in sports medicine and performance.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Anonymous emailed survey of AMSSM sports medicine physician members, with 333 completed responses (10.8% of opened emails), analysed with logistic and ordinal regression. 40.8% of respondents had recommended CBD and 24.8% cannabis for therapeutic purposes, mostly for musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain. Age, sex and practice setting were associated with attitudes toward cannabis legalisation, WADA and NCAA policy, and whether cannabis is seen as performance-enhancing.
records.limitations: The sample is physicians, not athletes, so the paper reports prescriber attitudes and self-reported recommendations rather than athlete outcomes. It is a single survey with a 10.8% response rate, sampling about 7% of AMSSM membership.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading physician attitudes or recommendation rates as evidence that CBD or cannabis helps athletes perform or recover, when the study measured neither effects nor athlete use.

changes: limitations: added a second abstract vs results conflict -> abstract 'Male physicians and younger physicians were less likely to identify cannabis as performance-enhancing', while the Results report only 'Male physicians were less likely ... (OR 0.38 ...)' and no age effect for that outcome
verification.residualConcerns: Cannabinoid recommendation content (medication-adjacent); the record stays at physician attitudes and makes no efficacy claims.

records.sourceFile: Planning the microcycle in elite football - To rest or not to rest.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective observational analysis of 56 team seasons from 18 elite football teams (1578 players and 2865 injuries in the full data set) from January 2018 to December 2021, using a shared data platform; the injury analysis was restricted to each team's 15 main outfield players (511 players, 965 time-loss injuries, 559 noncontact). The authors report that in 3- and 7-day turnarounds, sequences with the day off-feet at D+2 were associated with 2 to 3 times lower noncontact injury rates than no day off or a day off at D+1, and that differences between sequences were unclear for other turnaround lengths.
records.limitations: The design is observational and univariate, so it cannot separate day-off timing from workload, minutes played or player profile, and the D+2 sequences had the fewest observations (for example 18 of 655 three-day turnarounds). Off-feet days were inferred from missing exposure records, all authors are employed by Kitman Labs, the company that supplied the data platform, and the first author was an associate editor of the journal.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may treat the D+2 pattern as a cause of fewer injuries, but the study is observational and reports the effect in different ways across the abstract, results and discussion.

changes: evidenceSummary/methods: full data set (1578 players, 2865 injuries) presented as the analyzed sample -> added the analyzed subset ('511 main players and 965 time loss injuries, including 559 noncontact ones')

paper.findings: added that the 3-day x/o/x sequence (n = 18) had no noncontact training injuries and no match injuries ('There were no match injuries at all for turnarounds with a day off-feet at D + 2')
paper.findings: added that a day off per se showed no clear association ('differences ... between turnarounds with and without a day off-feet were unclear')
paper.limitations: added turnaround count inconsistency (methods '1871 turnarounds', Table 1 rows sum to 2203, Table 2 'Totals 2005') and the conclusion's 'moderate to large' wording
screeningLimitations: added low D+2 counts and editor conflict ('Buchheit was an associate editor of IJSPP at the time of submission')
verification.residualConcerns: Effect-size descriptions for the D+2 association vary across abstract, results, discussion and conclusion, and the turnaround totals do not reconcile; the 3-day D+2 estimate rests on 18 turnarounds with zero injuries. Reviewer should check Figure 2 if available.

records.sourceFile: Platelet-rich plasma injection for the treatment of hamstring injuries - A systematic review and meta-analysis with best-worst case analysis.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 clinical studies (published 2013 to 2018, searched to August 2018) of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection for hamstring injuries, with 207 PRP-group and 149 control-group hamstring injuries as protocol. The authors found no statistically significant difference in time to return to play or reinjury rate between PRP plus physical therapy (PT) and PT alone or no treatment, and mean complication rates were low.
records.limitations: The 10 studies were heterogeneous, poorly reported for PRP preparation and protocol, and included retrospective designs, with several studies losing more than 2 patients to follow-up. The results are short-term (mean follow-up 9.1 months) and cannot establish effects by injury grade or PRP type.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the non-significant point estimates (for example the 5.7-day faster return to play or the 0.82 best-case reinjury risk ratio) as evidence that PRP works would overstate a result the authors describe as statistically nonsignificant.

changes: paper.citation: '2020;1-9' used the online-first page range with placeholder volume ('AJSM Vol. XX, No. X, XXXX') -> year only
paper.methods: Coleman score described as an extraction tool -> quality appraisal ('quality of evidence was evaluated with the Coleman Methodology Score')
paper.findings: 'complications averaged 5.2% per study' -> four complications across four studies, mean rate 5.2% ('This totaled 4 complications')
verification.residualConcerns: Abstract reports a significant fixed-effects return-to-play difference (-5.70 days) while the results section and Figure 2 report a non-significant random-effects estimate (-5.67 days, P=.11). Record follows the results section; confirm against the published version.

records.sourceFile: Platelet-rich plasma shortens return to play in NFL players with acute hamstring injuries.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective single-team cohort of 108 NFL players with MRI-confirmed hamstring injury from 2009 to 2018, of whom 69 had grade 2 injuries: 30 received leukocyte-poor PRP plus standard rehabilitation and 39 received rehabilitation alone. The authors report no significant difference in days or practices missed (22.5 vs 25.7 days, P=.81; 18.2 vs 22.8 practices, P=.68) but 1.3 vs 2.9 games missed (P<.05) in the PRP group.
records.limitations: Treatment was chosen by the player and team, so groups differed in season timing and injury severity, and the study was retrospective and underpowered for days and practices. The one significant result is a single-game difference in one team's cohort, and reinjury (one case per group) cannot be compared.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the title's claim that PRP shortens return to play as a general finding would overstate it, because days and practices missed did not differ significantly and the only significant result was a one-game difference.

changes: paper.limitations: added conflict of interest ('J.P.B. has received ... royalties from Arthrex'; injections used the Arthrex ACP system)
paper.findings: added in-season subset result (PRP n=21 vs 29; only games missed significant, P<.05)

records.sourceFile: Playing Experience and Position     Influence Injury Risk Among NCAA Division I Collegiate Footballers.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective two-season cohort of 76 male NCAA Division I football players (101 player-seasons, 2014 and 2015), with injuries recorded by athletic training staff and exposure measured as training minutes or game snaps. Using Poisson mixed models with magnitude-based inference, the authors report that seniors had likely higher time-loss training injury risk than freshmen (RR 1.79, 90% CL 1.04 to 3.10), and that wide receivers had likely higher non-time-loss game injury risk (RR 1.84, 90% CL 1.01 to 3.36).
records.limitations: The study is from one program over two seasons, with only 27 games and small position groups (5 to 19 players), so most comparisons are unclear and some game time-loss estimates have confidence limits from under 1 to over 25. Injury was defined as any physical complaint, and physical qualities, collision exposure and training content were not measured.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the 'likely' results as firm risk ratios, such as the 5.08 for juniors in time-loss game injuries (90% CL 0.88 to 29.41), would overstate them because the intervals are very wide and the authors call several explanations speculative.

changes: paper.limitations: '(P values from 0.07 to 0.99)' attached to the 'likely' effects was misleading; the 'likely' effects in Tables 3-6 have P 0.07 to 0.21 -> corrected
paper.limitations: confirmed abstract wide receiver game finding is non-time-loss only (Table 3 WR RR 1.84 'Likely'; Table 4 WR RR 0.95 'Unclear')
paper.findings: added QB and TE likely lower training risk (Tables 5-6) for completeness
verification.residualConcerns: Accepted manuscript (IJSPP 2017) with no volume or pages printed; citation should be completed from the published issue.

records.sourceFile: Playing Rule Article Eight Decreases the Rate of Sport Related Concussion in NFL Players Over Two Seasons.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective pre-post review of NFL players placed on public injury reports for concussion in the 2016-2017 to 2019-2020 regular seasons (479 concussions), comparing the two seasons before and the two after playing rule article 8 (in force from 2018-2019). The authors report fewer concussions after the rule (3.3 vs 5.5 per 1,000 athlete exposures; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.73), with no significant change in games missed per concussion or in players placed on injury reserve.
records.limitations: Injuries were identified from public injury reports and cross-checked against game statistics, without medical records, severity or diagnosis data, and the design has no concurrent control group. Other NFL changes at the same time, including an educational program, and possible reporting differences could account for part of the drop.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the 40% lower rate as proof that the helmet-hit rule caused the decline would overstate it, because this uncontrolled pre-post comparison cannot exclude concurrent NFL education efforts or reporting changes, and the authors' own comparison with NFL-published rates shows a smaller decrease (RR 0.77).

changes: paper.findings/limitations: position P values come from t tests on seasonal counts (Table 2 'P Value - T Test'; two seasons per cohort), not exposure-adjusted rates, uncorrected ('We choose not to perform a Bonferroni correction') -> stated explicitly
paper.limitations: added the NFL vs study rate figures ('6.6 versus 5.5, and 5.1 versus 3.3 per 1,000 AEs')
paper.practicalImplications: removed team-level monitoring advice not derived from the findings; added that position results are too fragile to guide planning
verification.residualConcerns: Concussion topic. Accepted author version (Physician Sportsmed, online 14 Oct 2020) with no volume or pages printed; citation should be completed from the published issue. The authors' discussion states causally that the rule 'has significantly lowered concussion rate but not severity', which the uncontrolled pre-post design does not support; the record avoids that wording.

records.sourceFile: Playing football on artificial turf as a risk factor for fifth metatarsal stress fracture - A retrospective cohort study.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective cohort using a computer-based survey of 1,854 competitive football players aged 12 to 51 in Japan, of whom 41 had a physician-diagnosed fifth metatarsal stress fracture (MT-5) in the prior 24 months. In generalized estimating equation models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, playing hours, MT-5 history and spike cleat type, playing more than 80% of time on artificial turf was associated with higher odds of MT-5 than playing 0-20% (OR 3.44, 95% CI 1.65 to 7.18), while 61-80% clay time was associated with lower odds (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.59).
records.limitations: Surface exposure and injury were both self-reported over 24 months, which allows recall bias, and only 41 cases were available, so the estimates are imprecise. Confounders such as vitamin D and calcium intake were not modeled, and three of the four clay-time category estimates were not significant, so the protective clay finding rests on one category.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 3.44 odds ratio as proof that turf causes fifth metatarsal fractures and restrict turf training, when the design is observational and the surface effect was not isolated from other MT-5 drivers.

changes: paper.methods: GEE covariate list omitted years of play -> added ('age, sex, a history of MT-5, body mass index (BMI), years of play, playing hours per year and types of spike cleats')

paper.limitations: framed univariate OR 3.18 vs adjusted OR 3.44 as a conflict, which it is not -> replaced with the real Discussion vs Table 1 age conflict ('the MT-5 group was significantly younger' vs Table 1 19.68 vs 18.64, p=0.088) and the non-significant clay OR 0.42 (p=0.084)
screeningLimitations: 'several clay-time estimates were not significant' -> 'three of the four clay-time category estimates' (Table 3 GEE p=0.791, 0.062, 0.084; only 61-80% p=0.001)
paper.findings: listed only two non-significant clay ORs -> notes all other clay categories non-significant and adds the BMI association reported in Table 3 (OR 1.15, p=0.048)

records.sourceFile: Poor Sleep Quality’s Association With Soccer Injuries- Preliminary Data.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective cohort of 23 male elite soccer players from two first-division Brazilian clubs. Sleep was measured with wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries over 10 preseason days, and injuries were logged by club medical staff over 6 months; sleep efficiency was negatively correlated with absence time, severity and injury count (Spearman r from -0.49 to -0.69), and WASO was positively correlated with severity and injury count. Players classed as poor sleepers (n = 18) averaged 2.56 injuries and 29.4 days absent, versus 1.00 injury and 4.6 days for good sleepers (n = 5).
records.limitations: Nineteen of 42 invited players were excluded (7 with sleep complaints, 12 with incomplete actigraphy), and sleep was measured for only 10 preseason days while injuries were tracked for 6 months. The good-sleep group had only 5 players, so the group comparisons are unstable.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the sleep-injury links as causal and use sleep efficiency as an injury predictor for individual players, when this is a small observational study that did not account for training load or psychological and hormonal factors.

changes: paper.findings: omitted the significant sleep latency correlation and the null sleep duration result -> added (Table 1 'Sleep latency ... r = .449, P = .03'; sleep duration P = .24 to .46)

paper.limitations: added that the Discussion uses causal language ('these variables presenting a cause and effect relationship') despite the observational design; kept the confirmed Discussion vs Table 3 absence mismatch (17.5/5.0 vs 29.39/4.60 days) and stated that Table 3 values are used
verification.residualConcerns: Year 2019 is the ahead-of-print copyright year ('(c) 2019 Human Kinetics', downloaded 12/17/19); no issue year is printed.

records.sourceFile: Poor hamstrings to quadriceps torque ratios in male soccer players - weak hamstrings, strong quadriceps, or both.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional isokinetic study of 101 male soccer players (202 legs; 52 professional and 49 under-20) tested at 60 degrees per second in the first two weeks of preseason. Legs below each conventional and functional hamstrings-to-quadriceps cut-point had lower hamstring torque, with larger effect sizes for hamstring than for quadriceps torque, and the authors conclude that hamstring deficit is the key factor in low ratios.
records.limitations: A single-speed, single-session cross-sectional test with no injury outcome, so the study cannot show that the ratios predict or cause injury even though the authors discuss prevention. Inference: because the groups are defined by the ratio itself, part of the group difference is built into the comparison, which limits how far the 'hamstrings are the cause' conclusion can be read.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read a low hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio as proof that hamstring weakness causes injury and prescribe hamstring work from one preseason test, when the study measured neither injuries nor change over time.

changes: populations: added Healthy Athletes (players not in full training due to injury were excluded; included players were 'considered recovered by the medical departments')

paper.limitations: replaced the minor wording-error note with the substantive Table 2 inconsistency at the 0.90 cut-point ('n = 174' + 'n = 49' of 202 legs; balanced Q PT '256.55 +/- 37.04' identical to Table 1 0.60 row; ES 0.51 with p = 0.522)

records.sourceFile: Possible relationship between the gut leaky syndrome and musculoskeletal injuries - The important role of gut microbiota as indirect modulator.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Review of gut microbiota, intestinal permeability (leaky gut) and musculoskeletal injury, based on a keyword search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus with no reported selection criteria, study counts or quality appraisal. The authors state that the cited evidence is mostly observational, that longitudinal studies do not exist, and that many mechanistic links come from animal models; no studies were pooled. Conclusions are mechanistic and hypothesis-generating, linking gut permeability to systemic inflammation, pain sensitivity and tendon, bone and joint change.
records.limitations: The review does not grade or pool studies, and most of the evidence it cites is observational or from animal models, so causal links from gut permeability to athlete injury are not established. Athlete-specific data are sparse and the authors state that generalizability to elite or recreational athletes is unclear.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could over-read the proposed chain from gut permeability to inflammation to injury and recovery, or treat the authors' lifestyle and supplement recommendations as tested interventions for injury prevention.

changes: studyDesign: Narrative Review -> Systematic Review / Meta-analysis (a database keyword search is described: 'We searched the available literature in Pubmed/Medline, Web of Science, and Sport Discus using the terms...'; library precedent and INSTRUCTIONS rule)

evidenceSummary/methods: said the authors state no pooled sample or effect size was calculated, which the text does not say -> describes the search as having no reported selection criteria, study counts or appraisal; added authors' note that strategies are 'also based on the long practical experiences of the authors'
abstract/tldr: 'narrative review' wording removed to match the recoded design
athleteDev: 'mechanistic reasoning and mouse data' -> mouse data and an observational study in older adults ('older people with higher muscular performance presented high levels of genus Prevotella')
verification.residualConcerns: Design coded Systematic Review / Meta-analysis by library precedent only; the search is a bare keyword list with no selection, flow or appraisal, so in substance this is a narrative review. Operator may prefer Narrative Review.

records.sourceFile: Postinjury alcohol use is associated with prolonged recovery after concussion in NCAA athletes.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective observational study from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium (2014 to 2021) of 484 NCAA athletes with concussion and complete data, 104 of whom reported alcohol use after injury and 380 of whom did not. The adjusted mean time to unrestricted return to play was 23.3 days (95% CI 20.0 to 27.2) for the alcohol group and 17.7 days for the no-alcohol group (IRR 1.32, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.55, P<0.001), while SCAT3 symptom severity, headache and concentration or memory scores did not differ between groups.
records.limitations: The design is observational and alcohol, tobacco and marijuana use were self-reported without standardized drink size or timing, so causation cannot be inferred. Only 484 of 4,802 concussed athletes had complete data, included athletes differed from the full cohort in age, sex, previous concussions and baseline symptoms, and the alcohol group had more loss of consciousness, premorbid drinking and postinjury marijuana and tobacco use, none of which entered the return-to-play model.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the longer time to clearance as proof that avoiding alcohol after concussion shortens recovery, when the authors state that causality cannot be determined from this observational design.

changes: paper.methods: covariates confirmed as age, delayed symptom reporting and contact level ('Age, delayed reporting of symptoms, and level of contact were determined to be confounders'); added the >=1 drink per week exposure definition and the selection procedure

paper.limitations/screeningLimitations: unadjusted between-group differences made specific (LOC 10.6% vs 3.7%, P=0.005; premorbid drinking, marijuana, tobacco); added selection bias vs the original population ('similar except for statistically significant differences in age, sex, number of previous concussions, and SCAT3 symptom severity baseline scores') and few drinkers above 5 drinks per week
paper.limitations: confirmed Abstract vs Results CI conflict (16.1-19.3 vs 16.2-19.4) and the Abstract P-value misprint; Table 2 symptom P values 0.47 to 0.98
verification.residualConcerns: Concussion return-to-play paper: clinically sensitive. The association could be confounded by premorbid drinking, LOC and other substance use that were not in the final model.

records.sourceFile: Practices and perceptions in hamstring training for injury risk mitigation - A survey-based mixed-methods analysis.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Anonymous online mixed-methods survey of 47 practitioners (strength and conditioning coaches, sports therapists, physiotherapists, scientists and others) who work on hamstring injury risk across sports. Most reported programming Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) and high-speed running in both seasons, with off-season NHE and non-NHE upper-end volumes higher than in-season, though only the non-NHE upper-end difference was statistically significant (g = -0.70, p = 0.014). Thematic analysis identified compliance, multidisciplinary team coordination and time as the main challenges.
records.limitations: This is a self-selected, social-media survey of practitioners, not a measure of athlete training or injury outcomes. Several volume differences are non-significant, and the open-ended themes are descriptive.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the self-reported volumes as proof that practitioners over-dose the NHE or that their hamstring programmes are ineffective, when the survey measured neither injury nor adaptation outcomes.

changes: abstract: 'Practitioners said their NHE volumes are likely still above the smallest effective doses' -> this is the authors' conclusion from the reported volumes; added that NHE seasonal differences were non-significant (g = -0.44, p = 0.100; g = -0.42, p = 0.140)

limitations: added the discussion/abstract conflict ('A key observation from the study is the consistent volume of NHEs programmed during both the off-season and in-season'); HSR claim restated as untested frequency and descriptive data rather than 'largely non-numerical'
verification.residualConcerns: Methods-analysis mismatch (paired t-tests stated, but unequal group sizes and Hedges g used) means the reported p-values are of uncertain validity.

records.sourceFile: Pre-existing Lumbar Spine Diagnosis as a Predictor of Outcomes in National Football League Athletes.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective matched cohort of 2965 athletes at one NFL franchise's Scouting Combine (2003 to 2011), of whom 414 had a pre-existing lumbar spine diagnosis. The 253 drafted athletes with a diagnosis were matched to 323 drafted controls by age, position, year and round, and career statistics and a position-specific performance score were compared. Diagnosed athletes were less often drafted (61.1% vs 80.2%) and had fewer years played (4.0 vs 4.3), games played (46.5 vs 50.8) and games started (28.1 vs 30.6), with no difference in performance score (1.4 vs 1.8, P = .13).
records.limitations: This is a retrospective review of one franchise's combine records, using imaging reports, with career data taken from public sources. Only 2 drafted players had a lumbar fusion, so the fusion findings are anecdotal.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the reported draft and longevity differences as causal evidence that a lumbar diagnosis shortens NFL careers, or as a basis for fusion-related clearance decisions, when the design is retrospective and the fusion sample is two players.

changes: limitations: confirmed spondylolysis longevity conflict (text/abstract 'P = .01' vs Table 6 P = .32 years, P = .11 games) and years-played P mismatch (text .001 vs Table 4 .0001); added the quarterback exception and implausible Table 10 draft percentages
verification.residualConcerns: Spondylolysis longevity claim in abstract and conclusion is not supported by Table 6 values; Table 10 draft percentages look internally inconsistent. Spine-condition and contact clearance context makes this clinically sensitive.

records.sourceFile: Prehospital management of exertional heat stroke at sports competitions - IOC adverse weather impact expert working group for the Olympic Games Tokyo 2020.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Consensus statement by the International Olympic Committee Adverse Weather Impact Expert Working Group for Tokyo 2020, summarising prehospital management of exertional heat stroke at competitions. It sets out a designated on-site heat deck with cold water immersion, rectal temperature confirmation, and four-person treatment teams. The statement reports no new data and cites earlier race-medicine studies reporting 100% survival and about 93% discharge home on the day of collapse when athletes were cooled within 30 minutes.
records.limitations: A consensus document with no new data, written by members of the expert group, so its recommendations reflect the group's judgement of the evidence rather than a systematic review. It excludes Paralympic athletes, and the authors say procedures may need adapting to each sport and national medical service.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the heat deck and cooling steps as a validated protocol with proven outcomes, when the statement reports no new data and the outcome figures it cites come from earlier observational race-medicine reports.

changes: practicalImplications: added two omitted safety steps from the algorithm text: 'medical providers must first exclude any cardiac cause' and 'Collapsed athletes with confirmed hyperthermia below 40.5°C should still be cooled using the whole-body rotating ice-wet towel procedure'

records.sourceFile: Preinjury and postinjury factors that predict sports-related concussion and clinical recovery time.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective cohort of 1,152 Ivy League collegiate athletes (69% male) tested before the season with the SCAT3, mood screens, ImPACT and a self-reported risk-factor history, then followed for concussion. Only sport type and self-reported concussion history were associated with a later concussion (10%, 16% and 21% concussed with none, one and two or more prior concussions). In the 138 athletes followed to symptom resolution, no preinjury factor or baseline measure was associated with days to symptom-free or return to play, while post-injury symptoms and some ImPACT measures were correlated with longer recovery.
records.limitations: Ivy League athletes only, with self-reported risk factors, and only 34 women among the 138 concussed athletes, so sex differences could not be tested with much power. Post-injury findings are correlations in one cohort and were not tested as a prediction model in new athletes.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the post-injury symptom and ImPACT correlations as a tool that predicts an individual athlete's return-to-play date, when the study reports associations in one Ivy League cohort and proposes no decision rule.

changes: methods: 'SCAT3 within 1 day and ImPACT within 2 days of injury' misread the Table 6 acute-subgroup definition -> mean 0.83 and 2.48 days, range 0-13 ('Mean time from concussion to postinjury SCAT3 testing was 0.83 ... range 0-13 days')
findings: added that SCAT3 symptom total/severity were not significantly correlated with days to full RTP (Table 6: 0.18, 0.17) while ImPACT symptom, visual motor and reaction time were
screeningLimitations/limitations: 'single institution' not stated in text -> 'Ivy League athletes only' ('This study only examined Ivy League athletes')

records.sourceFile: Preliminary brain-behavioral neural correlates of anterior cruciate ligament injury risk land biomechanics using a novel bilateral leg press neu.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Preliminary fMRI study of 30 female high school soccer players (mean age 15.8 years), who performed a bilateral leg press in the scanner and a drop vertical jump with 3D motion analysis. Greater landing knee abduction moment was associated with greater activity in lingual gyrus, intracalcarine, posterior cingulate and precuneus regions, and a high-risk group (n = 4) showed more activity than a low-risk group (n = 5) in motor and visual regions. The authors describe the results as preliminary and report no effect sizes.
records.limitations: Thirty athletes in the correlation analysis and only four to five per group in the threshold analysis, all female, performing a supine bilateral leg press rather than a landing. Effect sizes were withheld by design, so the strength of the associations cannot be judged.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read these brain-activity patterns as a screening tool or validated neural marker of ACL injury risk, when the study is preliminary, uses four and five athletes per group, and reports no effect sizes.

changes: limitations: competing interest misattributed to Grooms -> Myer ('GDM consults with Commercial entities'; 'Dr. Myer is an inventor of biofeedback technologies ... and receives licensing royalties'); DRG lists only NIH and DoD funding
verification.residualConcerns: High-risk group size conflicts in the source (n = 4 in Table 1 and Methods, n = 5 in Table 2), and the low-risk cut-off is 6.0 Nm in text but 10.6 Nm in the Table 1 caption; both are noted in limitations.

records.sourceFile: Premorbid risk factors and acute injury characteristics of sport-related concussion across the NCAA - Findings from the CARE Consortium.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective cohort analysis of NCAA student athletes at CARE Consortium sites (baseline assessments 2014 to 2021) comparing 1,804 athletes with a sport-related concussion (SRC) against 21,702 without, across 22 sports. Unadjusted odds ratios showed higher SRC odds with prior SRC (one prior SRC: male OR 2.09, female OR 2.63), learning disorder (OR 1.50), ADHD (OR 1.38), and Black (OR 1.61) or multiracial (OR 1.32) identity compared with White athletes; depression was associated only in female athletes (OR 1.54) and migraine in both sexes. Among SRCs, 49.6% had altered mental status, 31.2% had delayed symptom onset, and injury characteristics differed by sex and contact level.
records.limitations: Unadjusted, observational odds ratios from a set of CARE sites with self-reported history and no control for athlete exposure, so the associations cannot predict individual concussion risk. Sports with fewer than 30 SRCs were excluded, and American football (male only, 34% of SRCs) dominates the contact category.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the race and sex associations as causal or as individual risk markers, when they may reflect sport participation mix, NCAA division and reporting differences.
